title: Question 1.1 (Butler et al.)
statement_text: Does there exist a constant $\alpha > 0$ independent of $n$, such that $HG(K_{n,n}) \geq n^\alpha$ for sufficiently large $n$?
context_text: Butler et al. posed this question in 2008 following results showing $\Omega(\log n) = HG(K_{n,n}) \leq n+1$. It asks whether the hat guessing number of the complete bipartite graph $K_{n,n}$ grows as at least a fixed positive power of $n$, despite having clique number only 2.
paper_contribution: Answers affirmatively in a generalized sense by proving $HG(K_{n,\ldots,n}) = \Omega\!\left(n^{\frac{r-1}{r}-o(1)}\right)$ for the complete $r$-partite graph with equal part sizes, implying in particular $HG(K_{n,n}) = \Omega\!\left(n^{\frac{1}{2}-o(1)}\right)$.
notes: Explicitly labelled Question 1.1 and attributed to Butler et al. [9] (2008). PDF source — exponent notation in surrounding display math may be garbled.
paper_title: The hat guessing number of graphs

title: Problem 1.4
statement_text: Do there exist functions $f_i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, $1 \leq i \leq 3$ such that (i) if the maximum degree of $G$ is $\Delta$, then $HG(G) \leq f_1(\Delta)$; (ii) if $G$ is $d$-degenerate, then $HG(G) \leq f_2(d)$; (iii) if the minimum degree of $G$ is $\delta$, then $HG(G) \geq f_3(\delta)$, and $f_3(\delta)$ tends to infinity when $\delta$ tends to infinity.
context_text: In the hat guessing game on a simple graph $G$, each vertex is a player who receives a hat colored arbitrarily with one of $q$ colors; each player sees exactly the hat colors of its neighbours (not its own), and all players simultaneously guess their own color according to a strategy agreed in advance, without communication. The players win if at least one guesses correctly for every hat assignment. The hat guessing number $\mathrm{HG}(G)$ is the largest $q$ for which a winning strategy exists ($G$ is then called $q$-solvable). Complete graphs, which have large hat guessing number, show that large cliques force large $\mathrm{HG}$, but $K_{n,n}$ has clique number $2$ and $\mathrm{HG}(K_{n,n})\to\infty$. Of the three functions, only $f_1$ is known to exist: by the Lovász Local Lemma $\mathrm{HG}(G)<e\Delta$ (folklore). Complete graphs and cycles suggest $f_1(\Delta)=\Delta+1$ might hold, and trees and complete bipartite graphs suggest $f_2(d)=d+1$, but it is not even clear whether $f_2$ exists. As partial progress on (ii), the authors show that if $G$ has a vertex of degree one and is $q$-solvable with $q\ge3$, then so is $G$ minus that vertex (so trees are not $3$-solvable, i.e. $f_2(1)\le2$), give a Local-Lemma bound $\mathrm{HG}(G)<ek^2q^k$ when the subgraph induced by the vertices of degree larger than $k$ is not $q$-solvable, and prove that the linear version (guessing functions affine over $\mathbb{F}_q$) satisfies $\mathrm{HG}_{lin}(G)\le d+1$ for $d$-degenerate $G$.
paper_title: The hat guessing number of graphs

title: Open question: exact value of $HG(K_{n,n})$
statement_text: What is the exact value of $HG(K_{n,n})$?
context_text: In the hat guessing game on a simple graph $G$, each vertex is a player who receives a hat colored arbitrarily with one of $q$ colors; each player sees exactly the hat colors of its neighbours (not its own), and all players simultaneously guess their own color according to a strategy agreed in advance, without communication. The players win if at least one guesses correctly for every hat assignment. The hat guessing number $\mathrm{HG}(G)$ is the largest $q$ for which a winning strategy exists ($G$ is then called $q$-solvable). Butler et al. showed $\mathrm{HG}(K_{n,n})=\Omega(\log\log n)$ and asked whether $\mathrm{HG}(K_{n,n})\ge n^{\alpha}$ for some constant $\alpha>0$; Gadouleau and Georgiou proved $\mathrm{HG}(K_{m,n})\le\min\{m+1,n+1\}$ and $\mathrm{HG}(K_{n,n})=\Omega(\log n)$. The authors answer the question of Butler et al. positively: more generally, the complete $r$-partite graph with $r-1$ parts of size $m=(2q\ln q)^{1/(r-1)}$ and one part of size $cr(q\ln q)^{r/(r-1)}$ is $q$-solvable, so the balanced complete $r$-partite graph satisfies $\mathrm{HG}\ge n^{(r-1)/r-o(1)}$. Hence $\Omega(n^{1/2-o(1)})=\mathrm{HG}(K_{n,n})\le n+1$, and determining the exact value is left open. They also ask whether $\mathrm{HG}(K_{g(q),q^c})\ge q$ for some $g(q)=o(q\ln q)$ and constant $c\ge1$, possibly $g(q)=\Theta(q)$.
notes: No labelled environment; stated as an open question in running prose immediately after Theorem 1.2.
